The salt-crusted radio had been dead for three years, so when it crackled to life at 2:17 a.m., Elias dropped his tea. The voice was his own, only younger — brighter, unbruised.

"Don't take the boat out," it said. "The storm turns at the last minute. I'm you, and I'm telling you: stay."

Elias gripped the desk. "This is a joke. Hollis, if you're —"

"It's not Hollis. Hollis is why you're listening. He's the one who dies."

The tea pooled around his boots. Outside, the sea was flat as slate, the gulls quiet. Every instrument in the tower read calm.

"You're a liar," Elias said, "or a ghost."

"I'm a forecast," the voice said, almost gently. "I'm what you become if you go. I've been sending this message every night for eleven years. You never answer. You just leave."

Elias laughed — a dry, terrible sound. "So I'm to believe a machine?"

"You're to believe yourself."
